title: Part Design & DFM
description: Part-level design and manufacturability review covering CAD hygiene, general part design, and process rules for molding, sheet metal, machining, casting, additive, extrusion, elastomers, cosmetics and volume production.

items.text: Every sketch and feature in released part models is fully constrained
items.hint: Check the feature tree for under-defined sketches (minus sign or blue geometry in most CAD tools). Under-defined sketches move silently when a dimension upstream changes.

items.text: The feature tree captures design intent: key dimensions drive the model and follow-on features reference them, not arbitrary edges
items.hint: Change a primary dimension (wall, overall length, boss spacing) and confirm the model updates sensibly. Models built on incidental edges fail or distort on the first ECO.

items.text: The model rebuilds with no errors, warnings or suppressed features left unexplained
items.hint: Force a full rebuild and review the error list. Suppressed or failed features can hide geometry that the supplier never sees in the STEP.

items.text: Part bodies are single, closed solids with no zero-thickness geometry, slivers or self-intersections
items.hint: Run the CAD geometry check (e.g. Check Entity / Validate Body) and an import check on the exported STEP. Broken geometry stops CAM, mold design and mold-flow meshing.

items.text: Model units are millimeters and the part origin and principal planes follow the project convention
items.hint: Check document units and confirm the origin sits on a meaningful datum (assembly origin or primary datum). Inconsistent units or origins cause scaled or misplaced parts at suppliers.

items.text: Modeled geometry is at nominal (or the agreed target such as mid-tolerance), and the convention is stated
items.hint: Suppliers cut steel and program CAM from the model. If some features are modeled at a limit and others at nominal, state the rule on the drawing or in the model notes.

items.text: No imported dumb solids or orphaned reference geometry remain in released part files
items.hint: Remove or hide construction bodies, surface leftovers and imported reference parts, or move them to a clearly labeled folder. Stray bodies get exported and quoted as real parts.

items.text: The material is assigned in the model and matches the material callout on the drawing and BOM
items.hint: Open the material property in CAD and compare with the drawing title block and BOM. A default material gives wrong mass, wrong FEA and wrong quotes.

items.text: Mass properties (mass, center of gravity) are checked against the budget and a sanity estimate
items.hint: Read the CAD mass properties with the correct material density and compare with the mass budget. A large mismatch usually means a missing feature, wrong material or wrong units.

items.text: Part file names, part numbers and revision properties follow the project numbering scheme
items.hint: Check the custom properties that populate the title block and BOM. Mismatched names and numbers cause wrong parts to be quoted or built.

items.text: Configurations or variants in the part file are named clearly and the released one is unambiguous
items.hint: Confirm which configuration is exported and drawn. Exporting the wrong configuration (e.g. a simplified or prototype variant) is a common release error.

items.text: Internal corners carrying load or bending stress have a radius, not a sharp corner
items.hint: Inspect the model with a curvature or edge check for zero-radius internal edges in load paths. Sharp internal corners are the most common origin of cracks in plastic, cast and machined parts.

items.text: Stress concentrations at holes, notches, section changes and snap roots are identified and relieved
items.hint: Mark the load path on the part and review every geometric discontinuity along it. Use the FEA from the analysis checklist to confirm peak stress where it matters.

items.text: Minimum wall, rib, hole and slot sizes are within the chosen process capability
items.hint: Compare the thinnest and smallest features (use thickness analysis in CAD) with supplier or process design guides. Features below capability are either not made or made inconsistently.

items.text: Features that locate the part to its mating parts are explicit (pins, bosses, slots), not reliant on outer profile
items.hint: Trace how the part is located in the assembly in each direction. Locating on cosmetic outer surfaces or on drafted walls gives poor repeatability.

items.text: The part has a defined location and method for part marking (part number, revision, material ID, date code, cavity ID as required)
items.hint: Check the model for a marking pad or engraving area and confirm the method (molded-in, laser, label, stamp) suits the process and is not on a Class A surface.

items.text: Features are oriented so the part can be made in the minimum number of setups, tool directions or forming steps
items.hint: Review the direction of every feature against the tool pull, spindle or press direction. Each extra direction adds a side action, setup or operation.

items.text: The part is not over-designed: thickness, features and precision are no more than the function needs
items.hint: Challenge every thick section, tight tolerance and secondary operation in the review. Over-design drives mass, cycle time and cost without improving function.

items.text: The part cannot be installed upside down or reversed if that would cause a failure, or misorientation is obvious
items.hint: Check symmetric-looking parts for asymmetric function. Add a poka-yoke feature where needed; the assembly checklist owns the assembly sequence itself.

items.text: Edges a user or assembler touches are broken or radiused, with no sharp edges or burrs left by design
items.hint: Review handled edges in the model and on the drawing for radius or chamfer callouts. Sharp edges are an injury risk and a common safety-review finding.

items.text: The selected manufacturing process for each part matches the production volume, cost target and geometry
items.hint: Record the process for each part and the reason (e.g. machined for pilot, molded for volume). A process mismatch found late forces redesign of the part.

items.text: Parts that change process between prototype and production have a design intended for the production process
items.hint: A part designed for machining or printing rarely molds or casts without changes to walls, draft and corners. Confirm the production design is the one being reviewed.

items.text: Clearances to mating parts, cables and moving parts are checked by interference detection in the assembly
items.hint: Run interference and clearance checks in the top-level assembly, including at motion extremes. Zero-clearance contacts that are not intended are flagged.

sections.title: Injection Molding: Walls, Draft, Ribs & Bosses

items.text: Nominal wall thickness is uniform across the part, within the range the resin design guide recommends
items.hint: Run a CAD thickness analysis and color-map the part. Rule of thumb: keep walls within about +/-10-15% of nominal; thick spots sink and void, thin spots short-shot.

items.text: Wall thickness transitions are gradual, not step changes
items.hint: Rule of thumb: taper transitions over a length of about three times the thickness change. Abrupt steps cause sink, warp, flow hesitation and stress concentration.

items.text: Every face parallel to the draw direction has draft
items.hint: Run a draft analysis for the pull direction of each half and every side action. Zero-draft faces scuff, stick or need costly tool changes. Rule of thumb: 1° or more per side for untextured surfaces.

items.text: Textured faces have draft sized for the specified texture depth
items.hint: Get the required draft per texture from the texture supplier or molder. Rule of thumb: about 1° per side extra for each 0.025 mm of texture depth; too little draft drags and streaks the texture.

items.text: Draft direction is chosen so critical dimensions and fits are controlled where they matter
items.hint: Decide whether a fit or seal dimension is controlled at the top or base of the draft and note it on the drawing. Draft can eat most of a tight clearance on tall walls.

items.text: Rib thickness is a fraction of the adjoining wall thickness to avoid sink
items.hint: Rule of thumb: rib thickness 40-60% of the wall, lower for high-shrink or cosmetic parts; check the resin design guide. Thick ribs sink on the opposite face.

items.text: Rib height and spacing are within moldable limits
items.hint: Rule of thumb: rib height no more than about three times wall thickness and spacing at least two times wall thickness. Tall thin ribs short-shot, stick in the tool and are hard to cool.

items.text: Ribs and walls have a root radius
items.hint: Rule of thumb: root radius about 25-50% of wall thickness. No radius concentrates stress; too large a radius creates a thick spot that sinks.

items.text: Bosses are cored out so their wall matches the nominal wall guideline
items.hint: Rule of thumb: boss wall about 50-70% of nominal wall. Solid bosses sink, void and lengthen cycle time.

items.text: Tall or loaded bosses are supported by gussets or connected to nearby walls with ribs
items.hint: Freestanding bosses crack, lean and fill poorly. Connect them with ribs or gussets that follow the rib thickness rule.

items.text: Bosses near walls are attached to the wall by a rib, or spaced away, not merged into a thick section
items.hint: Merging a boss into a wall creates a thick spot. Check thickness analysis around every boss.

items.text: Screw boss dimensions (hole, outer diameter, depth) follow the fastener supplier guide for the resin
items.hint: Thread-forming screw suppliers publish boss geometry per resin. Wrong pilot size strips or cracks bosses; confirm with a torque-to-strip test (see the validation checklist).

items.text: Holes and cores are sized and spaced to resist core deflection and breakage
items.hint: Rule of thumb: blind core length no more than about two to three times diameter for small cores; check with the molder. Long slender cores bend under melt pressure.

items.text: Thick sections that cannot be avoided are cored out from the non-cosmetic side
items.hint: Check thickness analysis for local thick spots at boss bases, corners and intersections. Core them out to the nominal wall where possible.

items.text: Sink and void risk areas are identified and accepted or eliminated
items.hint: Use thickness analysis and mold-flow sink prediction. Agree with the molder which areas may show sink and whether they matter functionally or cosmetically.

items.text: Outside corners have a radius equal to the inside radius plus wall thickness
items.hint: Concentric radii keep the wall uniform through the corner. Sharp outside with radiused inside (or the reverse) creates thick or thin spots.

items.text: Holes and windows near edges leave enough material for flow and strength
items.hint: Rule of thumb: hole-to-edge and hole-to-hole distance at least two times wall thickness. Narrow webs short-shot, knit badly and crack.

items.text: The resin supplier's design guide has been reviewed for the selected grade
items.hint: Most resin suppliers publish design guides covering walls, ribs, bosses, snaps and shrink. Note any recommendation the design departs from and why.

items.text: Parting line location is agreed with the molder and shown on the model or drawing
items.hint: Review the parting line with the toolmaker before kick-off. A late parting-line change is a tooling recut.

items.text: Gate location and type are agreed with the molder for each part
items.hint: Confirm the gate type (edge, sub, hot tip, valve) and location against fill, cosmetics and degating. Gate location drives knit lines, warp and fiber orientation.

items.text: Weld/knit lines are predicted and are not in high-stress areas
items.hint: Use mold-flow results to locate knit lines and overlay them on the load path. Knit lines can be far weaker than the bulk material, especially in glass-filled resins.

items.text: Ejector pin locations are agreed with the molder and avoid cosmetic and sealing faces
items.hint: Ask the toolmaker for an ejector layout. Witness marks and pin height tolerance (proud or recessed) must be acceptable where they land.

items.text: Ejection is feasible: the part has enough flat area or ribs for ejectors and will not stick on the wrong half
items.hint: Deep cores, low draft and textures on the ejector side cause sticking and distortion. Confirm with the toolmaker which half the part stays on.

items.text: Every undercut is justified, and the side action, lifter or collapsible core needed for it is agreed with the toolmaker
items.hint: List all undercuts from a draft analysis. Each action adds tool cost, maintenance and cycle time; remove undercuts that a pass-through core or redesign can avoid.

items.text: Lifters and slides have travel space and do not hit other features during ejection
items.hint: Ask the toolmaker to confirm travel and clearance for each action. Lifters need clear space behind the undercut equal to their travel.

items.text: Shut-off surfaces have adequate angle to avoid galling and flash
items.hint: Rule of thumb: shut-offs at least about 3-5° from the pull direction, per toolmaker preference. Vertical shut-offs wear quickly and flash.

items.text: Features likely to need tuning are designed steel-safe
items.hint: Model critical fits so that tuning removes steel (adds plastic): e.g. snap engagement, boss diameters and mating clearances. Adding steel is costly welding.

items.text: Shrink rate used for the tool is agreed with the molder for the specific resin grade
items.hint: Get the shrink value from the resin datasheet and molder experience, including flow and cross-flow values for filled resins. Wrong shrink scales every dimension.

items.text: Warp risk is assessed, including anisotropic shrink in glass- or fiber-filled resins
items.hint: Filled resins shrink differently along and across flow. Use mold-flow warp prediction for long, flat or thin parts and adjust gating or geometry.

items.text: Mold-flow analysis is done for critical, large, thin-walled or cosmetic parts
items.hint: Review fill, pack, weld lines, air traps, sink and warp. Run it before tool steel is cut; skip only for small simple parts where the molder agrees.

items.text: Air traps are identified and venting is planned at end of fill
items.hint: Mold-flow air-trap results and the toolmaker's venting plan should agree. Unvented ends of fill burn (dieseling) and short-shot.

items.text: Flow length to wall thickness ratio is within the resin's capability
items.hint: Check the resin's flow data or spiral-flow length for the nominal wall. Long thin flows need more gates or thicker walls.

items.text: Inserts or molded-in metal parts are designed for placement, retention in the tool and resin shrink around them
items.hint: Confirm insert loading method, tolerance and knurl or undercut for retention. Resin shrinking around metal can crack the boss; check the wall around the insert.

items.text: Multi-cavity or family tool layout is agreed, including cavity balancing and cavity ID marking
items.hint: Family tools fill unevenly when parts differ in volume. Add cavity numbers so defects can be traced.

items.text: Cooling and cycle time have been estimated for the thickest section and are consistent with the cost target
items.hint: Cycle time is roughly driven by the square of the thickest wall. Ask the molder for a cycle estimate and confirm critical cooling (e.g. inside deep cores).

items.text: Tool texture or polish spec is defined per surface, and draft supports it
items.hint: Specify texture or polish finish (e.g. a supplier texture code or SPI-style polish) for each face on the drawing or a texture map. Undefined finish is cut as the toolmaker sees fit.

sections.title: Injection Molding: Snaps, Hinges, Threads & Overmolds

items.text: Snap fits are moldable without side actions, or the action is justified
items.hint: Use pass-through cores or windows beneath hooks where possible. Each snap with its own lifter adds cost and maintenance.

items.text: Snap fits have a root radius and tapered beam where needed to spread strain
items.hint: A sharp snap root is a crack starter. A tapered beam lowers peak strain for the same deflection.

items.text: Snap retention force and disassembly behavior (permanent or releasable) match the requirement
items.hint: Check the return angle against the intended separation force. Confirm whether service removal is needed and how a technician releases the snap.

items.text: Living hinges use a resin suited to them and the geometry from the resin design guide
items.hint: Polypropylene and some PE grades are typical; most engineering resins fail quickly. Gate so flow crosses the hinge, and flex it right after molding if the guide says to.

items.text: Molded threads have a thread form, pitch and start suited to molding
items.hint: Molded external threads usually sit on the parting line or need unscrewing cores; internal threads need collapsible or unscrewing cores. Use coarse, rounded thread forms for plastic.

items.text: Threaded inserts (heat-staked, ultrasonic, press-fit or molded-in) have hole sizes and boss walls per the insert supplier
items.hint: Use the insert supplier's hole diameter and depth for the specific resin. Wrong hole size causes low pull-out torque or cracked bosses.

items.text: Heat stake and ultrasonic weld features follow the equipment supplier's joint design
items.hint: Check stake post diameter and height, energy director geometry and clearance for the horn. Poor joint design gives weak or flashy joints.

items.text: Overmolds have mechanical interlocks (through holes, undercuts, grooves) in addition to chemical bond
items.hint: Interlocks keep the overmold in place if the bond degrades from chemicals, heat or flexing.

items.text: Overmold shut-off edges on the substrate are designed for a clean seal of the second-shot tool
items.hint: The second shot needs a crisp shut-off groove or step on the substrate so it does not flash onto adjoining faces. Agree substrate tolerances with the molder.

items.text: Substrate is designed to withstand second-shot pressure and heat without deforming
items.hint: Thin substrate walls deflect under overmold pressure, causing flash and dimensional error. Support them from the tool side.

items.text: Press-fits into plastic have interference calculated against hoop stress and creep
items.hint: Calculate hoop stress at maximum interference and compare with the long-term allowable for the resin. Plastic press-fits relax over time and with temperature.

items.text: Bend radius is at least the minimum for the material, temper and thickness
items.hint: Check the supplier or material bend table. Rule of thumb: inside radius at least equal to thickness for mild steel; harder aluminum tempers need more. Too tight a radius cracks the outside of the bend.

items.text: Bend radii use the supplier's standard tooling where possible
items.hint: Ask the fabricator for their punch radius list. Non-standard radii mean special tooling or air-bend variation.

items.text: The flat pattern uses the supplier's K-factor or bend deduction for the material and tooling
items.hint: Get the K-factor or bend table from the fabricator and set it in CAD before releasing the flat. A wrong bend allowance shifts every formed dimension.

items.text: Holes and slots are far enough from bends to avoid distortion
items.hint: Rule of thumb: hole edge at least about 2-2.5 times thickness plus bend radius from the bend line. Closer holes deform into ovals during bending.

items.text: Bend reliefs are added where a bend meets an edge or another bend
items.hint: Check the flat for tears at bend ends. Rule of thumb: relief width at least sheet thickness and depth past the bend radius.

items.text: Flange length is at least the minimum for the press brake tooling
items.hint: Rule of thumb: minimum flange about 4 times thickness plus bend radius; confirm with the fabricator's die opening. Short flanges slip and bend unevenly.

items.text: Hems and teardrop hems have a radius or gap the material can form without cracking
items.hint: Closed hems crack in harder tempers and trap contamination. Confirm hem type with the fabricator and finish supplier.

items.text: Grain direction is specified where bends are tight or the material is prone to cracking
items.hint: Bending across the rolling direction tolerates tighter radii. Note the grain direction on the flat pattern if it matters.

items.text: Self-clinching hardware (PEM-style) is compatible with sheet thickness and hardness per the hardware supplier
items.hint: Check minimum sheet thickness, hardness and hole size in the supplier catalog. Fasteners in sheet that is too thin or too hard will not clinch.

items.text: Self-clinching hardware meets the supplier's minimum distance to edges and bends
items.hint: Use the supplier's centerline-to-edge values. Hardware too close to an edge bulges it; too close to a bend cannot be pressed after forming.

items.text: Countersinks are not specified in sheet thinner than the countersink depth requires
items.hint: In thin sheet a machined countersink leaves a knife edge. Use a dimpled (formed) countersink or a different fastener.

items.text: Tolerances across one or more bends reflect the fabricator's forming capability
items.hint: Tolerances across bends accumulate bend variation. Agree realistic values with the fabricator; dimension critical features within one flat face where possible.

items.text: Welds and spot welds are located where the welder can reach and distortion is acceptable
items.hint: Check electrode access for spot welds and torch access for fusion welds. Long welds near precise features distort them; plan post-weld machining if needed.

items.text: Finishing (plating, painting, powder coat) is specified after forming, or the coating is rated for forming
items.hint: Pre-plated or pre-painted sheet can crack at bends. Note whether finish is applied before or after forming and allow for coating thickness on fits.

items.text: Formed features (louvers, embosses, lances, extrusions) follow the fabricator's tooling dimensions
items.hint: Formed features need specific punch tooling. Use the fabricator's standard form tools where possible and keep them away from bends.

items.text: Flat pattern nests efficiently and the part avoids features needing secondary operations
items.hint: Ask the fabricator for nest yield on large parts. Tapped holes, machined features and deburring add operations.

items.text: Internal corner radii are no smaller than standard cutter radii, slightly larger than the cutter
items.hint: Rule of thumb: internal radius slightly larger than the cutter radius so the tool does not dwell in the corner. Sharp internal vertical corners need EDM.

items.text: Pocket depth is within the reach of a standard cutter for the corner radius
items.hint: Rule of thumb: pocket depth up to about 3-4 times tool diameter is routine; deeper needs long-reach tools, slow feeds and more cost.

items.text: Thin walls and floors are thick enough to machine without chatter or distortion
items.hint: Rule of thumb: about 0.8 mm minimum in metal and more in plastic, per machinist capability. Thin unsupported walls vibrate and spring after release.

items.text: Drilled holes use standard drill sizes unless a reamed or bored size is needed
items.hint: Match hole diameters to standard metric drills. Non-standard sizes need interpolation or special tools.

items.text: Tapped hole depth is no deeper than needed for thread engagement
items.hint: Rule of thumb: thread engagement about 1.5 times diameter in steel and 2 times in aluminum. Deeper threads add tap breakage risk and cost.

items.text: Blind tapped holes have drill depth beyond the full thread for tap clearance and chips
items.hint: Specify full-thread depth and drill depth separately. Bottom-tapping to the drill point breaks taps.

items.text: Threads in aluminum and other soft materials that are assembled repeatedly have threaded inserts
items.hint: Use wire thread inserts or key-locking inserts where screws are removed in service. Threads in soft metal strip after a few cycles.

items.text: Thread form, size and class are specified consistently in the model and on the drawing
items.hint: Use cosmetic thread features in CAD and check the drawing callout (e.g. M4x0.7-6H). Mismatched thread callouts cause wrong taps or mating hardware.

items.text: The part can be made in the minimum number of setups
items.hint: Count the faces that need machining and the orientations required. Each setup adds cost and a datum transfer that affects tolerances.

items.text: Every machined feature is accessible to a standard tool from a reachable direction
items.hint: Check for features hidden behind walls or needing angled access. Inaccessible features need 5-axis machining, special tools or redesign.

items.text: Edge breaks and deburr requirements are specified
items.hint: Add a general note for edge break (e.g. a small chamfer or radius maximum) and call out any edge that must stay sharp. Undefined deburring gives inconsistent parts.

items.text: Turned features have relief grooves at shoulders where threads or grinding end
items.hint: Thread runout and grinding wheels need a relief groove. Without one the thread is incomplete at the shoulder.

items.text: Turned parts have features concentric to one axis where possible to finish in one chucking
items.hint: Off-axis features and flats need mill-turn or a second operation. Group them where possible.

items.text: Raw stock size has been considered and the part does not waste a large stock size
items.hint: Check the envelope against standard bar and plate sizes. A part slightly larger than standard stock jumps to the next size.

items.text: Work-holding is feasible: the part has surfaces to clamp without distorting thin features
items.hint: Discuss fixturing with the machinist for thin or odd-shaped parts. Add sacrificial tabs if needed and note their removal.

items.text: Text and logos engraved or machined use a cutter-friendly font and size
items.hint: Small text needs tiny engraving tools. Rule of thumb: letter stroke widths larger than the smallest practical cutter; confirm with the shop.

items.text: Every face parallel to the die or mold pull has draft per foundry guidance
items.hint: Run draft analysis for the casting pull direction. Draft requirements differ for die casting, investment casting and sand casting; get them from the foundry.

items.text: Section thickness is as uniform as practical, with gradual transitions
items.hint: Thick sections solidify last and shrink, causing porosity and sink. Use thickness analysis and core out heavy areas.

items.text: All internal and external corners have fillets per foundry guidance
items.hint: Sharp corners cause hot tears, poor fill and stress concentration. Get the minimum fillet radius for the process from the foundry.

items.text: Parting line and gating are agreed with the foundry
items.hint: Parting line location affects draft, flash and trim. Gating and overflow location affect porosity and cosmetic areas.

items.text: Sealing faces and machined faces are located away from expected porosity
items.hint: Ask the foundry for solidification simulation or porosity experience. Porosity exposed by machining can leak through sealing faces; specify impregnation if needed.

items.text: Machined surfaces have machining stock added per foundry guidance
items.hint: Model the as-cast part with stock on machined faces and draw both as-cast and machined states. Too little stock leaves cast skin; too much exposes porosity.

items.text: Cored holes are sized and positioned within foundry capability, and holes needing precision are drilled after casting
items.hint: Small or deep cored holes need pins that break or bend. Specify drilled holes where position or size is tight.

items.text: Die-cast walls and ribs follow the die caster's rules of thumb for the alloy
items.hint: Get the die caster's minimum wall, rib and boss guidelines for the alloy (e.g. aluminum or zinc). Walls too thin cold-shut; too thick porous.

items.text: Casting datums and fixturing points for machining are defined on the as-cast part
items.hint: Define target datums on cast surfaces the machinist can locate from. Without them the first machining setup is improvised.

items.text: Ejector pin and overflow locations are acceptable for function and cosmetics
items.hint: Ask the die caster for ejector and overflow layout. Trimmed overflow and gate stubs need a place that does not affect fit or appearance.

items.text: As-cast surface finish expected from the process is acceptable or post-processing is specified
items.hint: Sand castings are rough and need machining or finishing on mating faces. State any shot blast, tumbling or coating requirement.

items.text: Pressure-tight castings have a leak test and impregnation requirement agreed with the foundry
items.hint: If the casting holds fluid or forms a sealed enclosure, specify the leak test and whether vacuum impregnation is allowed.

items.text: The additive process and material are chosen for the required strength, temperature, accuracy and finish
items.hint: Compare SLS, MJF, SLA, FDM and DMLS against the requirement with the service bureau. A process that cannot meet tolerance or temperature fails late.

items.text: Build orientation is defined for strength, accuracy and finish
items.hint: Layer lines are weak in FDM and somewhat in other processes. Orient so loads are not across layers and critical surfaces are not support faces.

items.text: Anisotropy of the printed material is considered in load-bearing features
items.hint: Use the service bureau's Z-direction properties for loads across layers. Many datasheets show only the best direction.

items.text: Minimum wall, hole and feature sizes follow the service bureau's design guide for the process
items.hint: Check thinnest features with CAD thickness analysis against the bureau's limits. Features below the limit print poorly or break during cleaning.

items.text: Support structures can be removed and support witness areas are acceptable
items.hint: Identify overhangs that need supports (SLA, FDM, DMLS). Supports inside closed channels cannot be removed.

items.text: Hollow or enclosed volumes have escape holes for trapped powder or resin
items.hint: SLS, MJF and SLA parts with sealed cavities trap powder or liquid resin. Add drain holes sized per the bureau.

items.text: Threads in printed parts use inserts or a thread form suited to the process
items.hint: Small printed threads are weak and inaccurate. Use heat-set inserts, tapped holes after printing or coarse modeled threads.

items.text: Dimensional accuracy expectations are agreed with the service bureau for critical features
items.hint: Get the bureau's accuracy statement for the process and part size. Plan post-machining for fits that need more.

items.text: Post-processing (support removal, curing, bead blast, dye, vapor smoothing, heat treat, HIP) is specified
items.hint: Post-processing changes dimensions, properties and appearance. Specify it on the drawing or purchase order.

items.text: Large flat areas and thick sections are designed to limit warp and residual stress
items.hint: SLS and DMLS parts warp with large flat areas or abrupt thickness changes. Add ribs, lattices or fillets per the bureau's advice.

items.text: Part design takes advantage of additive capability where it adds value (consolidation, internal channels, lattices)
items.hint: If the part is printed for production, check that it is not just a molded part design printed at high cost. Consolidation can remove fasteners and assembly steps.

items.text: Printed parts used for production have a defined material lot, machine and process qualification approach
items.hint: Print properties vary between machines, powder refresh rates and bureaus. Agree what is locked and how changes are controlled.

items.text: A standard extrusion profile has been considered before a custom die
items.hint: Check extruder catalogs for a standard profile that meets the need. Custom dies add tooling cost and lead time.

items.text: Custom profile walls are as symmetric and uniform as practical
items.hint: Unequal walls cool and flow unevenly, causing twist and dimensional problems. Rule of thumb: keep adjacent wall ratios within about 2:1.

items.text: Tongue ratios (depth to width of channels) are within the extruder's capability
items.hint: Deep narrow channels need a fragile die tongue. Ask the extruder for their maximum tongue ratio for the alloy.

items.text: Profile tolerances match the extruder's capability for the alloy and profile size
items.hint: Get the extruder's standard tolerances. Tighter tolerances require special processing or post-machining.

items.text: Cut length, end squareness and end machining are specified
items.hint: Saw cut length tolerance and burr are often looser than expected. Specify any end machining, drilling or deburr as a secondary operation.

items.text: Corner radii in the profile meet the extruder's minimums
items.hint: Sharp corners wear dies and cause tearing. Use the extruder's minimum internal and external radii.

items.text: Features along the length (holes, slots, cutouts) are designed for post-machining fixturing
items.hint: Long extrusions bow and twist within tolerance. Fixture locations and datum on the profile need definition.

items.text: Hollow profiles are designed for the die type the extruder recommends
items.hint: Hollow profiles need porthole or bridge dies with weld seams. Check the seam location is not in a highly stressed area.

items.text: Surface finish, anodizing and visible faces of the profile are defined
items.hint: Extrusion die lines are visible on exposed faces. Specify which faces are cosmetic and the finish requirement.

items.text: Durometer is selected for the function (sealing, damping, actuation, grip) and stated with its scale
items.hint: State hardness as Shore A or Shore 00 with a tolerance. Softer parts seal at lower force but extrude and tear more easily.

items.text: Gasket groove volume accommodates the compressed elastomer without overfilling
items.hint: Elastomers are nearly incompressible. Check groove fill at maximum material condition per the seal supplier guide.

items.text: Compression set data for the material at the operating temperature has been reviewed
items.hint: Look up compression set at temperature and time from the datasheet. High compression set means loss of sealing force over life.

items.text: LSR parts have shut-off, venting and parting-line clearances within the LSR molder's flash capability
items.hint: Liquid silicone flashes into gaps far smaller than thermoplastics do, so steel fits and venting must be agreed with the LSR molder. Flash on sealing or keypad faces is a common reject.

items.text: Keypad actuation force and travel meet the specification
items.hint: Model the membrane web and check the force-travel curve with the keypad supplier. Tactile ratio and travel drive user feel.

items.text: Elastomer parts have draft and parting line agreed with the molder, with flash location acceptable
items.hint: Elastomer parts are often demolded by stretching, but flash and parting line still need agreement. Flash on sealing faces leaks.

items.text: O-ring and seal dimensions use standard sizes where possible
items.hint: Use standard O-ring cross sections and sizes (e.g. ISO 3601 series). Custom sizes add tooling and lead time.

items.text: Elastomer parts are retained in position during assembly
items.hint: Loose gaskets fall out or twist during assembly. Use dovetail grooves, retention bumps or adhesive where needed.

items.text: Elastomer chemical compatibility with fluids, cleaners and greases it will meet is confirmed per supplier data
items.hint: Some elastomers swell or degrade in oils, alcohols or cleaners. Check the supplier compatibility chart.

items.text: Knit lines are predicted away from Class A surfaces
items.hint: Use mold-flow weld-line results overlaid on the cosmetic surface map. Knit lines on Class A faces show, especially with metallic or dark colors.

items.text: Sink marks are not expected on Class A surfaces
items.hint: Check rib, boss and thick-section locations behind cosmetic faces. Use mold-flow sink prediction and revise rib thickness if needed.

items.text: Gate vestige is hidden on a non-cosmetic face or under another part
items.hint: Agree gate location with the molder and check vestige height. A visible gate mark on a Class A face is a common cosmetic reject.

items.text: Parting lines are placed on edges or features where they are hidden or read as a design line
items.hint: A parting line across a flat cosmetic face shows mismatch and flash. Place it on a sharp edge or a design step.

items.text: Each cosmetic texture and gloss level is approved on a physical sample plaque before the tool is textured
items.hint: Approve texture, gloss and color on plaques in the production resin. Texture looks different on screen, in another resin or at a different draft; re-texturing a tool is slow and costly.

items.text: Class A, B and C surfaces are identified on the model or drawing
items.hint: Use a surface map or colored faces so the molder knows which faces are cosmetic. Without it, ejectors and gates may land on visible faces.

items.text: Matching parts have cosmetic gaps and flushness designed with realistic process variation
items.hint: Model nominal gaps large enough that variation does not cause interference or uneven gaps. Use a design step to hide mismatch at split lines.

items.text: Large flat cosmetic faces have slight curvature or texture to hide distortion
items.hint: Perfectly flat glossy faces show every warp and sink. A small crown or texture hides it.

items.text: Slide, lifter and tool insert witness lines are kept off Class A faces
items.hint: Review the tool layout with the toolmaker for every Class A face. Witness lines from actions and inserts show as fine lines and worsen as the tool wears.

items.text: Part cost drivers (material, cycle time, tooling, secondary operations) are reviewed against the cost target
items.hint: Get a cost breakdown from the supplier quote. Identify the top drivers and the design levers for each.

items.text: Tool life and steel specification match the lifetime volume
items.hint: Agree tool class and steel (e.g. hardened steel for high volume or glass-filled resin) with the toolmaker. Soft tools wear out early.

items.text: Supplier DFM feedback has been received for every new tool or production part
items.hint: Request a formal DFM report from each toolmaker or fabricator. Store it with the design record.

items.text: Every supplier DFM comment is dispositioned (accepted, rejected with reason, or deferred) and the record is kept
items.hint: Track DFM comments in a log with owner and decision. Unresolved comments resurface as tool changes.

items.text: Secondary operations (deburr, machining, inserts, painting) are minimized or justified
items.hint: List every post-process operation. Each adds cost, handling and a defect opportunity.

items.text: Number of cavities or production rate matches the demand forecast
items.hint: Compare cavitation or line capacity with annual volume and peak demand. Too few cavities limit supply; too many cost tooling up front.

items.text: Material grade is commonly available from more than one source or the single source is accepted
items.hint: Special grades and colors carry long lead times and minimum orders. Check availability with the supplier; the materials checklist owns the grade choice.

items.text: Design allows production tooling to be adjusted after first articles without a full recut
items.hint: Steel-safe fits, inserts for changeable features and adjustable stops allow tuning. Confirm with the toolmaker.

items.text: Part design supports automated handling, packing or inspection where planned
items.hint: Check for features that allow robot pick, nesting or vision inspection. Parts that tangle or nest poorly slow production.
